To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) B cell antigen presentation of intact HEL to naive HEL-specific CD4 T cells induces both B cell and T cell activation; (2) this response is radiation sensitive and requires the initial induction of CD28-dependent B7 costimulatory molecules by B cells; and (3) B cell antigen receptor signaling is required for the initial induction of the costimulatory B7 molecules.

B cells are required to activate naive CD 4+ T cells, that B cells are not the sole source of costimulatory molecules, and that resting, anergic, and tolerant B cells do not provide adequate costimulation for naive CD4+ helper T cells.

(i) naive CD4+ cells are activated by B7-1/2+ antigen presenting B cells; (ii) resting, anergic and tolerized B cells are defective as costimulators of naive CD4 T cells; and (iii) the ability of B cell to activate naive CD 4 T cells depends on both B cells antigen specificity and activation state.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between antigen-specific T and B cells and their role in the generation of antibody responses.
the molecular mechanisms underlying B cell antigen presentation, T cell activation, and the regulation of the immune response.
the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underly the development of T cell tolerance to self-antigens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the activation of naive T cells is a two-signal process, in that the T cells need both the antigen-specific signal from the T cell receptor and a second signal provided by the B cells, which is mediated by the B7 family of costimulatory molecules.
B cell antigen presentation can induce a form of "incomplete T cell activation" in the absence of costimulation.
B cells can present antigen to T cells and activate naive CD4 T cells, but only if they are nontolerant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability of a B cell to activate a naive T cell is dependent on both its antigen specificity and its activation state.
the activation state of B cells is critical for the ability to present antigen to naive CD4+ cells and induce a complete T cell activation response.
the activation state of the antigen presenting B cells determines the quality of the T cell response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
B cells can activate T cells, but only when they are in an appropriate activation state.
the B cell is a very important cell in the immune system.
the activation state of the B cell is a major determinant of its ability to activate naive T cells.
